content: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the leading cause of death globally, claiming more lives annually than any other condition. In 2019, out of 56 million deaths worldwide, 18 million were attributed to CVD. Hypertension (HTN) significantly increases the risk of diseases affecting the heart, brain, kidneys, and other organs. Approximately 1.28 billion people globally are affected by hypertension, yet only 23% of women and 18% of men have their condition under control. The guidelines for managing hypertension include eight key recommendations: 1. For individuals diagnosed with hypertension and a BP of ≥140/≥90 mmHg, treatment is strongly recommended based on moderate to high-certainty evidence. For individuals without CVD but with high CVD risk, diabetes, or chronic kidney disease (CKD) and an SBP of 130–139 mmHg, treatment is conditionally recommended based on moderate to high-certainty evidence. 2. Screening and Assessment Before Treatment: Tests to screen for comorbidities and assess cardiovascular risk should be conducted, but only if they do not delay the initiation of treatment. This recommendation is conditional and supported by low-certainty evidence. 3. Choice of Antihypertensive Drugs: The recommended drug classes include diuretics, ACE inhibitors (ACEi), angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs), and calcium channel blockers (CCBs). This is a strong recommendation based on high-certainty evidence. 4. Combination Therapy: To improve adherence and persistence, combination therapy is recommended, preferably in a single-pill formulation. This is a conditional recommendation supported by moderate-certainty evidence. 5. BP Targets for Hypertension Control: For individuals without comorbidities, the target BP is <140/90 mmHg. For those with CVD, the target SBP is <130 mmHg. For individuals with high CVD risk, diabetes, or CKD, the target SBP is <130 mmHg. These recommendations are strong and supported by moderate-certainty evidence. 6. Follow-Up Intervals: Monthly follow-ups are recommended until the target BP is achieved. Once the target BP is reached, follow-ups every 3–6 months are advised. These are conditional recommendations based on low-certainty evidence. 7. Involvement of Non-Physician Healthcare Workers: Trained non-physician healthcare professionals can provide hypertension treatment if they are granted prescribing authority, follow management protocols, and work under physician oversight. This is a conditional recommendation supported by low-certainty evidence. These guidelines are published by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 2022, with both electronic and print versions available under specific ISBNs. Some rights are reserved by the WHO.
